title: Files, folders and the terminal
lesson:
Programs keep their data in **memory** (RAM) while they run, and RAM is wiped when the program ends or the power goes. To keep anything, a program writes it to a **file** on a drive. Files live in **folders**, and every file has a **path** that says where it is: `D:\Archie\Workshop\notes.txt` on Windows, `/home/pi/notes.txt` on a Raspberry Pi.

A **relative path** like `notes.txt` means "in the folder the program is running in". That's the simplest, and what these exercises use.

Writing and reading a text file in Python:

```
with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("first line\n")
with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())
```

`"w"` means write (it replaces anything already there); `"a"` means append (add to the end); no letter means read. `\n` is the **newline** character, the invisible thing that ends a line. `with` closes the file for you when the indented part finishes, even if there's an error. `encoding="utf-8"` makes sure Swahili, accents and everything else are stored right.

The **terminal** (also called the command line) is a window where you type commands instead of clicking. `cd folder` moves into a folder, `dir` (Windows) or `ls` (Linux, Mac, Pi) lists what's there, and `python file.py` runs a program. VSCodium has one built in: Terminal → New Terminal. Everything a mouse can do, the terminal can do, and it's how you'll work with Raspberry Pis and servers.

example.code:
with open("diary.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Planted maize\n")
with open("diary.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("It rained\n")
with open("diary.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())
notes: Reading it back shows both lines.

exercises.title: Write and read
exercises.prompt: Write a program that creates shopping.txt with three lines (unga, sukari, chumvi), then reads the file back and prints what's in it.
exercises.starter:
# 1. open shopping.txt for writing and write three lines
# 2. open it again for reading and print it

tests.check:
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path(m.__file__).parent / 'shopping.txt'
assert p.exists(), 'shopping.txt was not created'
assert len(p.read_text(encoding='utf-8').strip().splitlines()) == 3, 'shopping.txt should have exactly three lines'
tests.name: the file has three lines

hints: Write each item followed by \n so they end up on separate lines.
Use with open("shopping.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: then f.write("unga\n") and so on.
exercises.solution:
with open("shopping.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("unga\n")
    f.write("sukari\n")
    f.write("chumvi\n")
with open("shopping.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

exercises.title: Add, don't replace
exercises.prompt: Write 'day 1' to log.txt with "w". Then, using append mode, add 'day 2' and 'day 3'. Print the file at the end: all three days must be there.

tests.check:
s = CODE
assert '"a"' in s or "'a'" in s, 'Use append mode ("a") for days 2 and 3'
tests.name: uses append mode

hints: "w" once at the start, then "a" to add.
Two with open(...) blocks: one with "w", one with "a", then one to read.
exercises.solution:
with open("log.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("day 1\n")
with open("log.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("day 2\n")
    f.write("day 3\n")
with open("log.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

quiz.q: What happens to a program's variables when the power goes out?
choices: They're lost unless written to a file
quiz.why: RAM is wiped; only files on a drive survive.

quiz.q: Which mode adds to the end of a file instead of replacing it?
What does the terminal command ls (or dir on Windows) do?
quiz.why: It lists the files and folders where you are.

cards.q: What does \n mean in a string?
cards.a: A newline: the end of a line.
It closes the file for you, even if there's an error.
A path from the folder the program runs in, like notes.txt.

explain: Explain files, folders and the terminal to someone who has never programmed, in your own words, with an example you make up (not one from the lesson).
